forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Enfield reports nil 2025/26 General Fund variance after £10.0m of government-approved support
news_drafts.lead:
Enfield Council's main account, the General Fund, ended 2025/26 with an overspend of £6.4m, which its outturn report (the actual figures once the year has ended) shows as nil after £10.0m of exceptional financial support and a £3.6m transfer to risk reserves. Exceptional financial support is government permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, and is a last resort. The Audit Committee on 2 November was given the figures. The gross variance was £14.5m before £6.7m of flexible capital receipts and £1.4m of reserve movements.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government formally approved the £10m in August 2026, after provisional approval earlier in the financial year. The council used £10m of capital receipts, applied to adult social care pressures, rather than drawing on reserves, money it has put aside. That brings its total support permission to £30m: £20.0m for 2024/25 and £10.0m for 2025/26.

Risk reserves stood at £46.2m at the end of 2025/26, against £36.2m before the support was applied. The council's minimum threshold for them was £43.3m, and the paper says it reached that threshold. The General Fund balance was increased to £17.7m, 5% of the 2025/26 net revenue budget. The external auditor's report states that "improvements in reserves were supported by Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)" and that debt levels continue to be high.

news_drafts.headline: Enfield secures 3% pension contribution saving from April
news_drafts.lead: Enfield Council will reduce its employer pension contributions by 3% from April 2026 following an independent financial assessment, known as an actuarial valuation, of the Enfield Pension Fund. The fund's net assets reached £1.71bn at 31 March 2026, having grown by £301m over the previous five years, confirming the improved funding position. However, the fund is now experiencing negative cashflow of approximately £2.0m annually, with pension benefit payments exceeding contribution income, reflecting the aging membership base and requiring active liquidity management.

findings.headline: The government estimated Enfield's core spending power increase under Fair Funding as the second highest in England and the highest in London.
findings.detail: The paper attributes this to the Fair Funding 2.0 review and says it gives certainty of funding for three years, though allocations for 2027/28 and 2028/29 are still expected annually.
findings.matters: The rank of a council's core spending power increase under the new funding system is something finance directors are comparing across the country.
findings.figures: Second highest core spending power increase in England; highest in London; funding certainty for three years
findings.quote: the government estimated that the borough has had the second highest increase in core spending power in the country and the highest in London.

findings.headline: Enfield's financial resilience is classed as "vulnerable", with the aim of moving to "stable" during 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper refers to the council's Financial Resilience Framework and states that attaining “resilient” status is within reach if financial discipline continues.
findings.matters: The council's own framework rating and its target for the next year is a benchmark other councils using the same kind of framework will read against.
findings.quote: The Council’s current financial resilience remains classed as “vulnerable”, with the aim of moving to “stable” during 2026/27.

findings.headline: The Medium-Term Financial Plan shows a balanced budget for the next three years, with a £34.5m gap in years four and five.
findings.detail: The paper says the 2026/27 net budget is £439.0m and that the first multi-year Settlement in a decade gives certainty for three years. It also states that budget gaps for 2029/30 to 2030/31 total around £35m.
findings.matters: A three-year balanced budget followed by a stated gap in later years is the medium-term profile other finance directors compare against their own forecasts.
findings.figures: £34.5m gap in years four and five; circa £35m budget gaps for 2029/30 to 2030/31; £439.0m 2026/27 net budget
findings.quote: The Medium-Term Financial Plan reflects that the Council will have a balanced budget for the next three years but a gap £34.5m remaining in years four and five.

findings.headline: Capital financing costs were 7.5% of the net revenue budget in 2025/26, below the 10-12% affordability range in the Capital Strategy, while the Capital Financing Requirement rose to £1,519m.
findings.detail: The paper says 14% of 2025/26 capital spend was funded from borrowing and 86% from non-borrowing sources. The CFR increase came from the HRA, and the General Fund CFR is £991m and HRA CFR £451m.
findings.matters: Capital financing costs against the stated affordability range, and the rise in the CFR, are measures other councils and lenders use to assess a council's borrowing burden.
findings.figures: 7.5% capital financing costs as share of net revenue budget; 10-12% affordability range; £1,488m to £1,519m CFR; £991m General Fund CFR; £451m HRA CFR; 14% of capital spend funded from borrowing
findings.quote: The proportion of net revenue budget allocated to total capital financing costs was 7.5% for 2025/26, which is below the affordability range of 10-12% established in the Capital Strategy.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure was £236.7m in 2025/26 against a revised budget of £493.8m, with temporary accommodation long leases at £26.7m against £189.8m.
findings.detail: The paper states the capital outturn will re-profile the programme, affecting 2025/26 and future budgets. Meridian Water regeneration spent £66.2m against £106.9m, and Council Dwellings spent £87.9m against £125.7m.
findings.matters: A capital outturn well below the revised budget, with the largest variance in long-leased temporary accommodation, is a re-profiling pattern that affects borrowing and future budgets.
findings.figures: £236.7m capital outturn; £493.8m revised capital budget; £26.7m temporary accommodation long leases against £189.8m; £66.2m Meridian Water against £106.9m; £87.9m Council Dwellings against £125.7m
findings.quote: The capital outturn will result in some re-profiling of the capital programme
